content: 1. A detailed description of the methodology used in the analysis should be documented and reported comprehensively. 2. The National Health Workforce Accounts (NHWA) Handbook provides a structured framework for monitoring and evaluating health workforce indicators. It includes modules on active health workforce stock, education and training, regulation and accreditation, education financing, and health labor market flows. 3. Health worker density is measured as the number of health workers per 10,000 population. This indicator is disaggregated by occupation and activity level, such as practicing health workers, professionally active health workers, and those licensed to practice. The total population is estimated using United Nations Statistics Division data. 4. Health worker distribution by age group is expressed as the percentage of active health workers in specific age categories, such as under 25, 25–34, 35–44, 45–54, 55–64, and 65 or older. This data is disaggregated by occupation. 5. The percentage of female health workers in the active workforce is calculated by dividing the number of active female health workers by the total number of active health workers (male and female). This indicator is also disaggregated by occupation. 6. Health worker distribution by facility ownership is measured as the percentage of active health workers employed in facilities categorized by ownership type (public, private not-for-profit, private for-profit). The classification aligns with institutional sector definitions from the System of National Accounts (SNA 2008). 7. Health worker distribution by facility type is expressed as the percentage of active health workers employed in specific facility types, such as hospitals, residential long-term care facilities, ambulatory health care providers, ancillary services, retailers (e.g., pharmacies), and providers of preventive care. This data is disaggregated by occupation. 8. The share of foreign-born health workers in the active workforce is calculated as the percentage of active health workers who were born abroad. This indicator captures the dependency on health workforce migration and is disaggregated by occupation. 9. The share of foreign-trained health workers in the active workforce is measured as the percentage of active health workers who received their training abroad. This indicator provides insights into the reliance on internationally trained professionals and is disaggregated by occupation. 10. Data reporting for these indicators is recommended on an annual basis. Potential data sources include health workforce registries, aggregate data from health facilities, professional council registers, labor force surveys, population census data, and health facility databases. 11. The NHWA Handbook emphasizes the importance of harmonizing data collection and reporting methodologies to ensure comparability across regions and countries. WHO recalculates health worker densities using standardized population data to achieve this goal. 12. Further information and references for these indicators are available from WHO publications, OECD reports, and other international organizations, which provide guidance on health workforce planning, monitoring, and evaluation.
